title: Relational model, keys, constraints, ER modelling
scopeHtml: Scope: tables and SQL model, surrogate vs natural keys, foreign keys, constraints, NULL logic, ER modelling and common schema smells. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: What a relational database is
notes.html:
A relational database stores facts in tables (rows and columns) and lets you combine tables by matching values. A table is a set of rows; every row has the same columns; each column has a type. The "relational" word comes from math (a relation is a set of tuples), not from "relationships between tables".

The big idea: you describe WHAT you want (SQL), and the database figures out HOW to get it (the planner, covered in file 05). That is why the same query can stay correct while the engine gets faster.

Worked example. A users table with 10M rows, each row about 120 bytes: 10M x 120 B = 1.2 GB of heap, plus indexes. Postgres stores it in 8 KB pages, about 60 to 65 rows per page after the row header (23 bytes) and alignment, so roughly 160,000 pages.

CREATE TABLE users (
  id         bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  email      text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('a@x.com'), ('b@x.com');
SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE email = 'a@x.com';

Industry examples. Postgres runs Instagram's core data (they famously sharded it), Notion and Stripe-class payment ledgers. MySQL (InnoDB) powers Facebook's TAO storage tier and Uber's Schemaless-on-MySQL. SQLite is the same model embedded in every Android phone, which you already use through Room.

Postgres vs MySQL. Both speak SQL. Postgres has richer types (arrays, jsonb, ranges), partial indexes and RETURNING. MySQL InnoDB stores rows inside the primary-key B+tree (clustered); Postgres stores rows in an unordered heap and all indexes point to it. This one difference explains many later behaviours.

Everyday analogy. A set of spreadsheets where each sheet has a strict header, and you can ask "show me every order together with the customer's name" without the spreadsheets knowing about each other in advance.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "relational means tables are related". It is the math term for a set of tuples.
  • Thinking SQL says how to run the query. It is declarative; the planner chooses.
  • Forgetting a table has no guaranteed row order without ORDER BY.

notes.title: Keys: candidate, primary, alternate, surrogate
notes.html:
A key is a column (or set of columns) whose value identifies exactly one row. A candidate key is any minimal set of columns that is unique. You pick one as the primary key (PK); the others are alternate keys (enforce with UNIQUE).

Natural key = a real-world value (email, passport number, ISBN). Surrogate key = an invented value with no meaning (bigint identity, UUID). Surrogates win in practice because real-world values change (people change emails), are sometimes reused, and are often long.

Surrogate type Size Good Bad
bigint identity 8 B Small, ordered, index-friendly Guessable, hard to generate across shards
UUID v4 (random) 16 B Generate anywhere, unguessable Random inserts scatter across the B+tree, causing page splits and cache misses
UUID v7 / ULID (time-ordered) 16 B Generate anywhere AND ordered Leaks creation time; v7 needs a recent Postgres/library 
-- Natural key kept as an alternate key, surrogate as PK
CREATE TABLE country (
  id   smallint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  iso2 char(2) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name text NOT NULL
);

Worked example. Insert 100M rows with random UUID v4 PKs in InnoDB (clustered): each insert lands on a random leaf page, so after the working set exceeds the buffer pool (say 16 GB), almost every insert is a disk read plus later a page split. Teams report big throughput drops versus an auto-increment key. In Postgres the heap is append-friendly but the PK index still suffers the same random-leaf problem.

Industry examples. Stripe-style prefixed IDs (cus_...) are surrogates with a type tag. Twitter Snowflake IDs are 64-bit, time-ordered and generated on many machines, solving the "ordered but distributed" problem. Instagram's sharded Postgres built its own 64-bit time+shard+sequence IDs.

Decision gravity. Choosing the PK type is close to a one-way door: it is copied into every foreign key and every child index. Changing int to bigint later means rewriting huge tables. Default to bigint (an int overflows at 2.1 billion; teams have been woken at 3 a.m. by that) unless you have a reason.

Everyday analogy. Your name is a natural key (can change, can duplicate). Your student roll number is a surrogate: meaningless but stable and unique.

Common interview traps.

  • Using int PK on a table that can pass 2.1 billion rows.
  • Using email as PK and then needing to change an email across 20 child tables.
  • Saying UUIDs are "always slower"; random v4 is the issue, ordered ones are fine.

notes.title: Foreign keys and referential integrity
notes.html:
A foreign key (FK) says: this column's value must exist as a key in another table (or be NULL). It stops orphans: an order pointing to a customer who does not exist.

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  total_cents bigint NOT NULL CHECK (total_cents >= 0)
);
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_idx ON orders(customer_id);  -- Postgres does NOT do this for you

ON DELETE actions. RESTRICT/NO ACTION (refuse), CASCADE (delete children too), SET NULL, SET DEFAULT. Cascade is convenient and dangerous: deleting one tenant row can silently delete millions of rows and lock for minutes.

Key detail. Postgres does not auto-create an index on the referencing (child) column. Without it, deleting a parent row scans the whole child table to check for references, and joins are slow. MySQL InnoDB does create one automatically.

Worked example. orders has 50M rows, no index on customer_id. DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 7 runs a sequential scan of orders (about 6 GB read, seconds) while holding locks. With the index it is a sub-millisecond lookup.

Industry examples. Large-scale shops often drop FKs on the hottest tables (Shopify and GitHub have discussed online-schema-change and sharding reasons) and enforce integrity in application code plus periodic audit queries. The trade: speed and easy sharding versus lost guarantees.

Decision gravity. Adding an FK later to a big table is expensive but possible in Postgres: ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (takes a weaker lock). Removing one is easy. So start with FKs; drop them deliberately when measured.

Everyday analogy. A library loan card that must refer to a real member. The FK is the librarian refusing to log a loan for a made-up person.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting to index the FK column in Postgres.
  • Using ON DELETE CASCADE on a multi-tenant root table.
  • Claiming FKs are "too slow"; the cost is usually one index lookup per write, and the cost of orphan data is higher.

notes.title: Constraints: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, EXCLUDE
notes.html:
Constraints are rules the database enforces on every write, no matter which app or script writes. They are your last line of defence against bugs; app-level validation can be bypassed by a second service or a manual fix.

Constraint Meaning
NOT NULL Value required
UNIQUE No duplicates (implemented with a unique index). NULLs are allowed multiple times in Postgres (NULLs are not equal); Postgres 15 added UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT
CHECK Any boolean expression on the row
PRIMARY KEY UNIQUE + NOT NULL
EXCLUDE (Postgres) No two rows may "overlap", for example two bookings for the same room and time range 
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;
CREATE TABLE booking (
  room   int,
  during tstzrange,
  EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, during WITH &&)
);
INSERT INTO booking VALUES (1, '[2026-01-01 10:00, 2026-01-01 11:00)');
INSERT INTO booking VALUES (1, '[2026-01-01 10:30, 2026-01-01 11:30)');
-- ERROR: conflicting key value violates exclusion constraint

Worked example (race condition fixed by a constraint). App code does "SELECT if email exists, else INSERT". Two requests 5 ms apart both see "not exists" and both insert: two accounts, same email. A UNIQUE (email) makes the second insert fail with SQLSTATE 23505, which the app turns into "email taken". Correctness comes from the constraint, not the check.

Industry examples. Payment systems use UNIQUE (idempotency_key) so a retried request cannot charge twice (Stripe documents idempotency keys for this reason). Booking systems use exclusion constraints or unique (resource, slot) rows.

MySQL differences. MySQL enforces CHECK only from 8.0.16; before that it parsed and ignored it. No EXCLUDE. A unique index allows multiple NULLs too.

Decision gravity. Constraints are cheap to add early and painful to add to dirty data later (you must clean violations first). Treat them as reversible only before data is dirty.

Everyday analogy. The bouncer at the door versus a polite sign saying "please be 18". The sign is app validation; the bouncer is the constraint.

Common interview traps.

  • Check-then-insert in application code without a unique constraint.
  • Assuming UNIQUE blocks duplicate NULLs.
  • Storing money in float; use integer cents or numeric.

notes.title: Nulls and three-valued logic
notes.html:
NULL means "unknown", not zero and not empty string. Comparisons with NULL give UNKNOWN (neither true nor false). A WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is TRUE.

SELECT NULL = NULL;            -- NULL (unknown), not true
SELECT NULL IS NULL;           -- true
SELECT 5 NOT IN (1, 2, NULL);  -- NULL, so the row is dropped!
SELECT COALESCE(phone, 'n/a') FROM users;

The famous trap. x NOT IN (subquery) returns nothing if the subquery yields even one NULL. Use NOT EXISTS instead. Aggregates ignore NULLs (COUNT(col) skips them, COUNT(*) does not); AVG over {10, NULL, 20} is 15, not 10.

Worked example. orders has 1,000 rows, 100 with coupon IS NULL. WHERE coupon <> 'SAVE10' returns only rows with a non-null coupon different from SAVE10, so those 100 are missing. Fix: WHERE coupon IS DISTINCT FROM 'SAVE10'.

Design view. Many NULLs in a column often hint that the column belongs in a separate table (an optional 1:1 child). Oracle treats empty string as NULL; Postgres and MySQL do not.

Everyday analogy. A form field left blank: "I don't know your age" is different from "your age is 0".

Common interview traps.

  • WHERE col = NULL (never matches). Use IS NULL.
  • NOT IN with a nullable subquery.
  • Forgetting COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) difference.

notes.title: Entity-relationship modelling
notes.html:
ER modelling is drawing the nouns (entities), their facts (attributes) and how they connect (relationships) before creating tables. Interviews love it because it shows you can turn vague requirements into a schema.

Steps: (1) list nouns: User, Order, Product. (2) decide each one's identity (PK). (3) decide cardinality of every relationship. (4) turn into tables.

Relationship Example Table design
1:1 user and profile FK with UNIQUE on child, or same PK
1:N customer and orders FK on the "many" side
M:N students and courses Junction table with two FKs and a composite PK 
CREATE TABLE order_item (
  order_id   bigint REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  product_id bigint REFERENCES product(id),
  qty        int NOT NULL CHECK (qty > 0),
  unit_price_cents bigint NOT NULL,    -- snapshot, not a live lookup
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);

Key design lessons. (a) Snapshot prices in order_item; the product's price changes later but the old order must not. (b) The junction table is itself an entity and often grows its own columns (qty, enrolled_at). (c) Model "state" with a status column plus a history table when audits matter. (d) Soft delete (deleted_at) breaks UNIQUE unless you use a partial unique index: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users(email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL.

Worked example. Ride-hailing sketch: rider, driver, trip(rider_id, driver_id, status, fare_cents), location_ping(driver_id, ts, lat, lon). Pings are 1 per 4 s per driver; for 500k active drivers that is 125k writes/s, far too hot for the main relational DB, so pings go to a time-series or log store while trip stays relational. Knowing what NOT to put in the relational core is a senior signal.

Industry examples. Uber's trips and Airbnb's bookings are relational cores; the high-volume streams live elsewhere. Shopify's famous orders/line_items model is exactly the junction pattern above.

Decision gravity. Cardinality mistakes are one-way-ish: turning 1:N into M:N later means a new table and a backfill with downtime planning. Ask "can one X ever have many Y?" for every line.

Everyday analogy. Planning a school: students, teachers, classes. A class has many students and a student many classes, so you need an enrolment register in the middle.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting product_name and price live-joined into historical orders.
  • Modelling M:N with a comma-separated column.
  • Forgetting to ask whether a relationship can change over time (a customer's address history).

notes.title: Beyond the basics: keys at scale and common smells
notes.html:
Composite keys vs surrogate. A junction table naturally uses a composite PK (order_id, product_id). Column order matters for index use (file 04). Many ORMs prefer a single surrogate column; both are fine.

Smells to name in interviews.

  • EAV (entity-attribute-value): one table of (entity, attr, value). Flexible, but no types, no constraints, painful joins. Prefer jsonb for the truly dynamic part.
  • Polymorphic FK: (owner_type, owner_id) can't have a real FK. Prefer one FK column per target, or separate tables.
  • Storing lists in a column: violates 1NF (file 02).
  • Enum as string everywhere: use a lookup table or Postgres enum / CHECK; enum values are hard to remove in Postgres.
-- jsonb for genuinely sparse attributes, relational for the rest
ALTER TABLE product ADD COLUMN attrs jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}';
CREATE INDEX product_attrs_gin ON product USING gin (attrs);
SELECT id FROM product WHERE attrs @> '{"color":"red"}';

Industry examples. Shopify and GitLab use jsonb/JSON columns for flexible settings but keep money, status and relations in typed columns. Wikipedia's MediaWiki schema is a long-lived relational design on MySQL.

Decision gravity. jsonb is reversible in a weak way (you can extract to columns later) but queries and constraints on it are weaker; use it for attributes you will not join or constrain on.

Everyday analogy. A form with fixed boxes (typed columns) plus one "notes" box (jsonb). Notes are flexible, but you can't make the bank check them.

Common interview traps.

  • Recommending EAV because "schema is flexible".
  • Polymorphic associations with no integrity.
  • Using jsonb for everything and losing constraints and statistics.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• A relational DB stores sets of typed rows; SQL is declarative, the planner chooses the plan.
  • Prefer a bigint (or time-ordered UUID) surrogate PK; keep natural keys as UNIQUE. PK type is a near one-way door.
  • Foreign keys prevent orphans; in Postgres index the child column yourself; avoid CASCADE on big roots.
  • Constraints (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, EXCLUDE) are the real correctness layer; they fix check-then-insert races.
  • NULL is unknown: use IS NULL, IS DISTINCT FROM, NOT EXISTS instead of NOT IN.
  • ER modelling: nouns, identity, cardinality; M:N needs a junction table; snapshot historical values.
  • Avoid EAV and polymorphic FKs; use jsonb only for sparse, unconstrained attributes.
